Advertising revenue funds Meta Platforms' AI spending. That equation leans entirely on ads, so the model's value to Meta Platforms runs through engagement and ad pricing. A model that increases engagement and supports higher ad prices is the path to a return on the investment.

A flat denial of takeover talk is lifting one of the biggest names in enterprise software. ServiceNow (NYSE:NOW) stock is up 5% to $146.93 in midday trading after the company rejected reports that it planned to buy Decagon, a privately held maker of artificial intelligence (AI) customer-service agents.

gorodenkoff / iStock via Getty Images

Meanwhile, Salesforce (NYSE:CRM) stock is up 4% to $245.39, a gain just shy of the advance in ServiceNow stock. Palantir Technologies (NASDAQ:PLTR) stock is down 0.9% to $199.07, moving opposite both of those software gainers. That split points to selective buying inside the enterprise software group.

Decagon Denial Sparks a Software Rally

ServiceNow moved to shut down the speculation on October 14. Amit Zavery, the company's president, chief product officer and chief operating officer, stated, "We are aware of misinformation in the market today about our acquisition strategy. Management also sees no major strategic gaps requiring large-scale deals at this time, according to Zavery. Because ServiceNow sells workflow software on recurring subscriptions, the denial of a big acquisition signals where ServiceNow's margins and product roadmap could be heading, and organic growth tends to keep spending tied to products ServiceNow controls end to end.

Bybit's xStocks tokens give non-US investors exposure to stocks like NVIDIA and Apple under the token issuer's rules, not a regulated broker's.

Finally! You can open a SoFi Crypto account and access 25 plus cryptocurrencies without juggling apps or logins.

Bybit announced on October 12, 2026, that users can now buy stocks with crypto, making it easier to trade more than 1,000 US-listed stocks and ETFs. The platform enables these trades using USD Coin (CRYPTO: USDC), a stablecoin designed to match the value of the US dollar.

However, it's essential to understand that "stock" can mean different things in crypto trading. One method involves sending a buyer's order to a US broker who holds the actual shares. In contrast, another method issues a token that tracks a company's shares, based on terms set by the token's creator.

PBXStudio / Shutterstock.com

Bybit specifies that USDC is the only cryptocurrency involved. So what do buyers actually own when they purchase stocks like Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) with crypto?

Bybit Routes Stock Orders Through Alpaca, a US Broker
Amal Kamal 17 / Shutterstock.com

When you buy stocks through Bybit, your orders are executed by Alpaca Securities LLC, a US broker that holds the underlying shares. Bybit offers popular stocks such as Apple, NVIDIA (NASDAQ: NVDA), Tesla (NASDAQ: TSLA), Micron Technology (NASDAQ: MU), and the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ: QQQ), which tracks the Nasdaq-100 index.

Users can pay for their stock purchases using USDC directly from their Bybit account, and fractional shares are available. This means buyers can own a portion of a stock without paying for a whole share.

------

START NOW: Finally! You can open a SoFi Crypto account and access 25+ cryptocurrencies without juggling apps or logins.

------

Trading runs 24 hours a day, five days a week, across US pre-market, regular, and after-hours sessions, depending on product availability. Bybit doesn't charge commissions on eligible trades, but its announcement doesn't spell out other fees.

Who Holds the Shares Bought on Bybit?
ConceptCafe / Shutterstock.com

Bybit clarifies that Alpaca executes the trades and maintains custody of the underlying stocks. As a self-clearing broker-dealer, Alpaca manages settlements and record-keeping internally. It is also a member of the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) and the Securities Investor Protection Corporation (SIPC), which safeguards customers' securities up to $500,000 in case a member broker fails.

The broad market exchange-traded fund SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) was down 0.3% and the actively traded Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) was 1.2% lower in Thursday's premarket activity amid a steady stream of economic data.

US stock futures were mixed, with S&P 500 Index futures down 0.3%, Dow Jones Industrial Average futures gaining 0.3%, and Nasdaq futures slipping 1.1% before the start of regular trading.

US initial jobless claims rose to a level of 199,000 in the week ended Oct. 10 from an upwardly revised 198,000 level in the previous week, compared with expectations for a level of 200,000 in survey of analysts compiled by Bloomberg as of 7:50 am ET.

The US Producer Price Index rose by 1.3% in September following a 0.5% increase in August, well above the 0.6% gain expected in a survey compiled by Bloomberg as of 7:50 am ET.

US retail sales rose by 0.8% in September, a larger increase than the 0.3% increase expected in a survey compiled by Bloomberg and following the previous month's revised 1.3% rise.

The New York Federal Reserve's Empire State manufacturing index rose to 25.5 in October from 7.6 in September, compared with a much smaller expected increase to a reading of 12.0 in a survey compiled by Bloomberg as of 7:50 am ET.

The Philadelphia Federal Reserve's monthly manufacturing index decreased to 20.9 in October after falling to 37.8 in September, compared with expectations for a smaller decrease to a reading of 28.0 in a survey compiled by Bloomberg, but still points to solid expansion.

August's business inventories data will be released at 10 am ET.

The weekly natural gas stocks data is slated for a 10:30 am ET release followed by the weekly crude oil stocks data at 12 pm ET.

Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh and Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack are the Fed speakers for Thursday.

Premarket trading is a thin session that runs before the 9:30 a.m. opening bell, so these readings can change before and after the open. Asia's losses have been far steeper than America's.

What Happened While You Were Asleep

The Economic Times reported that Japan's Nikkei index fell nearly 5% overnight. Moneycontrol reported that South Korea's KOSPI fell nearly 8%. Those outlets reported the numbers, which have not been independently verified. Both indexes trade overseas and appear here only as context.

Citing Reuters, The Economic Times linked the selling to concern over the financial health of a US cloud-computing provider and fears of higher interest rates after hotter-than-expected US inflation data. CNBC separately reported that worry about an AI borrowing binge was hitting that company's bonds. Inflation data supports that worry. Consumer prices rose 3.7% in September from a year earlier, according to government labor data.

Why Wall Street Is Holding Up Better Than Asia

The difference comes down to what each index holds, and most indexes weight companies by size, so whichever industries grow biggest end up taking over the index. A scare about AI hardware hits them hard. Japan's and South Korea's benchmarks are packed with chip and memory manufacturers and the equipment suppliers that serve them. The S&P 500 is more spread out. In one leading S&P 500 index fund, technology made up 38.0% of assets as of June 30. The rest included financials at 11.6%, health care at 8.9% and utilities at 2.2%. Banks, drugmakers and power companies have little to do with AI chip debt. The Nasdaq fund falls in between. Falling bond yields are failing to lift tech stocks, and Michael Burry is warning that the pain could persist. "The Big Short" investor highlighted a bearish "Red October" scenario that would gain conviction if the Magnificent Seven followed semiconductor shares lower alongside yields.

"Me about pain trades- pain trades become widowmaker trades because they tend to last a very long time," Burry said in a Substack chat.

S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) fell 1.1% to $769.60 on Wednesday, while Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) dropped 2% to $728.95 and the SPDR Dow Jones Industrial Average ETF Trust (DIA) slipped 0.1% to $515.63.

Falling Yields Offer Tech Little Relief

Burry highlighted a warning that tech stocks were failing to benefit from lower bond yields. "While the consensus view is lower yields = bullish stocks, the pain trade continues to be rates down, Nasdaq down."

The next test was whether weakness in semiconductor stocks would spread to the Magnificent Seven. "We have already seen semis fall with rates, but should we finally see Mag7 fall with rates, that would add conviction to our call for a 'Red October'."

The Magnificent Seven comprises Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta Platforms and Tesla. Burry highlighted the group's position as the market's "Last Man Standing" and flagged parallels between semiconductor stocks' recent performance and the period around the 2000 tech bubble. He also pointed to a possible failed breakout in the S&P 500 index.

Selling Pressure Tests Wall Street's Quiet Streak

Burry noted a pickup in trading activity after two-decade lows in volume, with the SPY trading about 15% above average volume and QQQ about 25% above average. The S&P 500 was nearing a 1% decline, while falling stocks accounted for 79% of NYSE volume.

He also highlighted the S&P 500's longest stretch without a 1% down day since 2020. The NYSE had gone nearly a year without declining stocks accounting for at least 80% of a session's volume, its longest such streak in records dating to 1996.

title: Invesco QQQ Doesn't Own a Single Bank, and That's Not the Only Thing the Nasdaq-100 Leaves Out
detail:
Invesco QQQ Doesn't Own a Single Bank, and That's Not the Only Thing the Nasdaq-100 Leaves Out
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Wed, October 14, 2026 at 4:43 PM PDT 5 min read
QQQ
JPM
WFC
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

JPMorgan Chase and Wells Fargo each released third-quarter results on Tuesday, and the two banks made more than $21 billion between them. JPMorgan's net income grew 6% year over year to $15.3 billion, and Wells Fargo's climbed around 6% to almost $6 billion.

Investors in the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) didn't own a slice of either one. The popular exchange-traded fund (ETF) tracks the Nasdaq-100, and the index doesn't admit banks -- or any other company classified as financial, for that matter.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

And banks aren't the only thing missing. Some of the biggest companies in the U.S. stock market are absent for a reason that has nothing to do with what they sell.

I don't think any of this is a reason to skip QQQ, which trades near $742 and has risen about 21% in 2026 as of this writing. But it's worth knowing what the fund leaves out before using it as a stand-in for the whole stock market.

Image source: JPMorgan Chase.

Two rules explain what's missing

The Nasdaq-100 is built to track 100 of the biggest non-financial companies listed on Nasdaq, and each half of that description acts as a rule. A company can't be classified as a financial business, and it must keep its primary listing on a Nasdaq exchange.

The first rule cuts out a big chunk of the market. Financials are the second-largest sector in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC), at around 11.5% of the index as of Oct. 12. QQQ, though, holds no banks and no insurers at all.

The second rule might go further than many investors realize. Berkshire Hathaway and Visa both trade on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE), so they're out no matter how they're classified. Oracle and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing are missing for the same reason, though both are tech companies.

Walmart shows how mechanical the listing rule can be. The retailer moved its shares from the NYSE to Nasdaq last December, and it joined the Nasdaq-100 in January. The business, of course, was the same as before -- just the listing changed.

Has skipping banks hurt returns?

Leaving out banks hasn't hurt QQQ's long-term returns. Its annual return for the 10 years through September was around 21%. The State Street Financial Select Sector SPDR ETF (NYSEMKT:XLF), which holds the S&P 500's financial stocks, averaged about 13% a year over the same span.
